effect_estimate.comment: Quantitative multivariable multilevel linear and logistic regression estimates plus weighted descriptive trends across 1993–2012 NSS waves.
effect_estimate.value: In the primary multilevel linear regression (N = 2,390 slums across 4 NSS waves in 10 states; weighted N = 168,901), each 1-year increase in legal notification is associated with a 0.768-point lower Basic Services Deprivation Score (BSDS, 0–100 scale where higher indicates worse deprivation; beta = -0.768, 95% CI: -0.914 to -0.622, p < 0.001; quadratic term beta = 0.009, 95% CI: 0.005 to 0.013, p < 0.001). Modeled dichotomously, notified slums score 10.546 points lower on BSDS than non-notified slums (beta = -10.546, 95% CI: -12.092 to -9.001, p < 0.001). Slums on central government land have higher deprivation than those on state/city government land (beta = 6.785, 95% CI: 3.480 to 10.089, p < 0.001), whereas slums on private land have lower deprivation (beta = -3.182, 95% CI: -4.880 to -1.483, p < 0.001), and lacking a community association is associated with higher deprivation (beta = 4.291, 95% CI: 2.622 to 5.961, p < 0.001). Between 1993 and 2012 in the 10 states, lack of piped water fell from 37.3% to 16.2% in notified slums while rising from 30.2% to 33.6% in non-notified slums; lack of septic/flush/pour-flush toilets fell from 61.6% to 27.7% in notified slums vs. 62.6% to 57.0% in non-notified slums; and lack of sewer infrastructure fell from 79.1% to 53.8% in notified slums vs. 85.0% to 82.0% in non-notified slums. In 2012 NSS multilevel logistic regression (N = 706 slums; weighted N = 28,635), non-notified slums had lower odds of receiving government slum-improvement financial aid than notified slums (OR = 0.379, 95% CI: 0.246 to 0.584, p < 0.001).

mechanism_certainty.comment: Observational repeated cross-sectional regression study appraised with JBI Cross-Sectional checklist (design ceiling = 2). Coded 1 (documented statistical association) because the NSS data document settlement-level statistical associations between legal notification status, land ownership, and service deprivation/aid receipt without directly observing administrative processing or refusal mechanisms (which are discussed from secondary case studies).

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines slum legal recognition/notification status conferring basic security of tenure (tenure), underlying land ownership across state/city government, central government, and private land (property), presence of a community slum improvement association (participation), intergovernmental jurisdictional barriers on central government land requiring no-objection certificates (institutional_fragmentation), and de facto exclusion of non-notified slums from JNNURM/RAY financial aid schemes despite no formal legal status bar.

sample_size.comment: Unit of analysis is the urban slum settlement. Additionally, NFHS-3 slum birth records (exact N not reported) were used in an auxiliary regression to derive alternative BSDS weights for sensitivity Table A3.
sample_size.value: 2,901 slum settlements across all states in 4 NSS waves (1,298,672 sampled slum households; weighted N = 190,557 slums / 33,280,053 households); 2,390 slum settlements with non-missing data across 10 largest states in primary regression and trend analyses (out of 2,411 slums in those 10 states; 1,109,693 sampled slum households; weighted N = 168,901 slums / 29,476,449 households); 706 slum settlements in 10 largest states in 2012 NSS financial support regression (weighted N = 28,635 slums)

study_design.comment: Authors explicitly note in Section 4(iv) that the NSS collects repeated cross-sectional settlement-level data rather than following the same slums longitudinally, and that the observational design cannot establish causality.
study_design.value: Repeated cross-sectional observational study analyzing four waves (1993, 2002, 2008–2009, 2012) of nationally representative slum settlement survey data (India National Sample Survey) using multivariable multilevel linear and logistic regression models (slums nested within states) and a state fixed-effects sensitivity model
